chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who loves some of his children more than others, and thus gives preference to one child over another. He said, 'Yes, Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) did that; he gifted Muhammad. And Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) did that; he gave something to Ahmad.'

I stood by him until I had memorized it for him, and I said, 'May I be your ransom, if a man loves his daughters more than his sons?' He said, 'Daughters and sons are equal in that; it is only according to the amount He (Allah) causes him to give from it.'

key_terms.الْأَشْعَرِيِّ: al-Ash'ari (a tribal designation for the narrator Sa'd)
key_terms.بِقَدَرِ مَا: according to the amount/measure of what
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a phrase of respect and readiness to serve)
key_terms.نَحَلَ: to gift or give a present

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a father to give more gifts to one child over another in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that a father’s preferential gifting (*nahlu*) to one child over another is permissible and was practiced by the Imams, distinguishing it from obligatory inheritance. It further establishes that this discretion applies equally to sons and daughters, as the gift is a voluntary act of the father’s choice rather than a divine decree, reflecting the Shia juristic view that equality in gifting is not mandatory but recommended for fairness.
